title: Kestrel and reverse proxies (nginx, IIS, load balancers)
hook: Kestrel is the web server inside your ASP.NET Core process. In production, nginx, IIS, or a cloud load balancer usually sits in front to handle TLS, connection limits, and routing.

blocks.text: Kestrel is ASP.NET Core's cross-platform web server. It reads HTTP requests from sockets, passes them through the middleware pipeline, and writes responses. It is fast and suitable for direct internet exposure in controlled scenarios, but production architectures almost always place a reverse proxy or API gateway in front. The proxy terminates Transport Layer Security (TLS), enforces rate limits, serves static files, and forwards requests to Kestrel over HTTP — often on localhost or an internal network.

entries.plainDefinition: The default in-process HTTP server for ASP.NET Core, implemented on top of libuv or sockets.
entries.example: Listens on http://0.0.0.0:8080 inside a Docker container.

entries.plainDefinition: A server that accepts client connections and forwards them to upstream application servers.
Encrypts HTTP traffic. Often terminated at the proxy, not inside Kestrel.
entries.example: AWS Application Load Balancer handles HTTPS; Kestrel sees plain HTTP.

entries.plainDefinition: X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto, and X-Forwarded-Host headers that preserve original client IP and scheme through a proxy.
entries.example: UseForwardedHeaders middleware so redirects use https:// not http://.

blocks.text: Running Kestrel alone behind a public IP works for demos but misses defense in depth. Proxies buffer slow clients, protect against slowloris attacks, and centralize certificate rotation. Misconfigured forwarded headers break OAuth redirects, rate limiting by client IP, and audit logs. In Kubernetes, the ingress controller is your reverse proxy; Kestrel binds to port 8080 on the pod while the ingress handles TLS and path routing to multiple services.

blocks.title: Production default
blocks.body: Kestrel handles application logic; the reverse proxy handles TLS, HTTP/2 edge features, and upstream load balancing across pods.

sections.heading: How it works step by step

blocks.title: Request path through proxy to Kestrel

items.title: Client sends HTTPS
items.body: Browser or mobile app hits api.example.com on port 443.

items.title: Proxy terminates TLS
items.body: nginx, IIS, or AWS API Gateway decrypts and may authenticate at the edge.

items.title: Forward to Kestrel
items.body: Proxy opens an HTTP connection to the upstream — often http://localhost:5000 or a pod IP.

items.title: ASP.NET Core pipeline
items.body: Middleware, routing, controller, Redis cache lookup, JSON response.

items.title: Response returns through proxy
items.body: Proxy may compress, add security headers, and re-encrypt for the client.

snippet.label: Configure Kestrel endpoints in Docker
snippet.explanation: Bind 0.0.0.0 so Docker and Kubernetes can reach the pod. TLS is usually off here — the ingress terminates HTTPS.

snippet.label: Forwarded headers for correct scheme and client IP
snippet.explanation: Without UseForwardedHeaders, HttpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress shows the proxy IP, not the client. Redirects may use http instead of https.

snippet.label: nginx upstream config (companion to Kestrel)
snippet.explanation: nginx sets forwarded headers Kestrel expects. keepalive reduces connection churn between proxy and upstream under high concurrency.

snippet.label: Kestrel limits for high-concurrency API behind gateway
snippet.explanation: Tune Kestrel limits together with API gateway timeouts. Mismatched timeouts cause 502 Bad Gateway errors that look like application bugs.

blocks.title: Edge server patterns
rows: Often nginx or cloud LB in front of Node
PM2 cluster mode forks Node workers

blocks.title: Pitfalls to avoid
blocks.body: Terminating TLS in both nginx and Kestrel without reason — double encryption overhead. Forgetting UseForwardedHeaders before UseHttpsRedirection — infinite redirect loops. Binding Kestrel to 127.0.0.1 in Docker so health probes from another network namespace fail. Assuming Kestrel replaces a CDN for static assets. Setting KnownProxies too loosely and allowing header spoofing.

blocks.text: How to prove it in production: compare RemoteIpAddress before and after UseForwardedHeaders in a staging ingress. Watch 502 rates when upstream keepalive pools exhaust — correlate nginx error log upstream timed out with Kestrel active connections via dotnet-counters (Microsoft-AspNetCore-Server-Kestrel). For WebSockets through a proxy, verify Upgrade and Connection headers pass through. API Gateway (AWS) adds latency budget — measure p95 at Kestrel versus at the edge with distributed tracing.

blocks.title: Kestrel direct versus behind proxy
rows: Cert rotation per app; fewer edge protections
Extra hop; must configure forwarded headers
Not recommended for public internet APIs

blocks.title: What gets you rejected in interviews
blocks.body: Saying 'IIS is required for ASP.NET Core' — Kestrel is the default cross-platform server. Claiming Kestrel cannot handle production load without nginx — it can, but proxies add operational benefits. Not knowing UseForwardedHeaders must run early in the pipeline. Recommending double HTTPS termination without measuring overhead.

interviewTakeaways: Kestrel is the in-process HTTP server; reverse proxies terminate TLS, load-balance, and protect upstream apps.
UseForwardedHeaders must be first middleware when behind nginx, IIS, or a load balancer — fixes IP, scheme, and redirect bugs.
In production, align Kestrel timeouts with API gateway/nginx timeouts; mismatch causes 502s under slow clients.

60s: Kestrel runs inside the process and handles HTTP. Production puts nginx or ALB in front for TLS and routing. Forward X-Forwarded-* headers. UseForwardedHeaders early. Kestrel binds internal port; proxy faces the internet. Tune limits together.
Follow-up: when would you terminate TLS in Kestrel instead of at the proxy?
commonPitfalls: Saying 'Kestrel is only for development' gets you rejected — it is the production server; the proxy is an optional but common edge layer.
Omitting UseForwardedHeaders — OAuth and IP-based rate limits break silently.
Strong answer: 'Kestrel serves the app. Proxy handles TLS and edge policy. Forward headers. Configure timeouts on both sides. Scale by replicating Kestrel processes behind the load balancer.'
introducedIn: Kestrel since ASP.NET Core 1.0; ForwardedHeaders middleware in ASP.NET Core 1.1

jsTsCorrelations.note: Express app.set('trust proxy', 1) reads X-Forwarded-For for req.ip — same problem as UseForwardedHeaders in ASP.NET Core.
NestJS apps also listen on an internal port while ingress handles TLS. The forwarded-header trust problem is identical across Node and Kestrel stacks.
